[[File:Human lineages Sima de los Huesos.png|thumb|upright=1.4|The relationships of the Sima de los Huesos hominins]]
In 2014, [[mitochondrial DNA]] (mtDNA) was extracted from Femur XIII, which suggested that this individual shares a closer common ancestor with Central Asian [[Denisovan]]s (the [[sister taxon|sister group]] of Neanderthals) than with Neanderthals.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=Matthias|last1=Meyer|first2=Qiaomei|last2=Fu|first3=Ayinuer|last3=Aximu-Petri|first4=Isabelle|last4=Glocke|title=A mitochondrial genome sequence of a hominin from Sima de los Huesos|journal=Nature|year= 2014|issn=1476-4687|pages=403–406|volume=505|issue=7483|doi=10.1038/nature12788|first5=Birgit|last5=Nickel|first6=Juan-Luis|last6=Arsuaga|first7=Ignacio|last7=Martínez|first8=Ana|last8=Gracia|first9=José María Bermúdez|last9=de Castro|first10=Eudald|last10=Carbonell|first11=Svante|last11=Pääbo|pmid=24305051 |bibcode=2014Natur.505..403M |url=https://eprints.ucm.es/id/eprint/27979/1/nature12788.pdf }}</ref> In 2016, [[nuclear DNA]] (nDNA) analysis instead concluded that the Sima de los Huesos hominins are more closely related to (but are not) Neanderthals. Because mtDNA is inherited from mother to child, the Sima de los Huesos hominins may carry the ancestral Neanderthal/Denisovan ("Neandersovan") mtDNA lineage, which was replaced in Neanderthals by interbreeding with African migrants sometime later.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=Matthias|last1=Meyer|first2=Juan-Luis|last2=Arsuaga|first3=Cesare|last3=de Filippo|first4=Sarah|last4=Nagel|title=Nuclear DNA sequences from the Middle Pleistocene Sima de los Huesos hominins|journal=Nature|year=2016|issn=1476-4687|pages=504–507|volume=531|issue=7595|doi=10.1038/nature17405|first5=Ayinuer|last5=Aximu-Petri|first6=Birgit|last6=Nickel|first7=Ignacio|last7=Martínez|first8=Ana|last8=Gracia|first9=José María Bermúdez|last9=de Castro|first10=Eudald|last10=Carbonell|first11=Bence|last11=Viola|first12=Janet|last12=Kelso|first13=Kay|last13=Prüfer|first14=Svante|last14=Pääbo|pmid=26976447 |bibcode=2016Natur.531..504M }}</ref>

Further discoveries of complete mandibles at the Sima de los Huesos indicate clear distinction from Mauer 1. While the Sima de los Huesos cranial and mandibular anatomy has developed most of the Neanderthal apomorphies (the earliest appearance for many of them in the fossil record), the rest of the skeleton retains many ancestral features ([[plesiomorphy and symplesiomorphy|plesiomorphies]]), and nDNA indicates that they are a distinct group. They are, nonetheless, firmly nested in the "Neanderthal [[clade]]". Their anatomy also suggests that many Neanderthal apomorphies evolved by the mid-Middle Pleistocene, and the rest appeared late near the beginning of the Late Pleistocene, maybe associated with the full [[speciation]] of ''H. neanderthalensis''.<ref name=QuamMartinez2024>{{cite journal|first1=Rolf|last1=Quam|first2=Ignacio|last2=Martínez|first3=Yoel|last3=Rak|first4=Bill|last4=Hylander|title=The Neandertal nature of the Atapuerca Sima de los Huesos mandibles|journal=The Anatomical Record|year=2024|issn=1932-8486|pages=2386–2388|volume=307|issue=7|doi=10.1002/ar.25190|doi-access=free|first5=Ana|last5=Pantoja|first6=Carlos|last6=Lorenzo|first7=Mercedes|last7=Conde-Valverde|first8=Brian|last8=Keeling|first9=María Cruz|last9=Ortega Martínez|first10=Juan Luis|last10=Arsuaga|pmid=36998196 }}</ref>

The Sima de los Huesos hominins can be grouped as "pre-Neanderthals",<ref name=Richards2021/> which can also include specimens from [[Montmaurin-La Niche mandible|Montamaurin-La Niche]], [[Bontnewydd Palaeolithic site|Pontnewydd]], Steinheim, Swanscombe, and [[Aroeira 3|Aroeira]]. This group may ultimately descend from a [[Near East]]ern source population which dispersed across Europe in the mid-Middle Pleistocene — maybe the same one represented at the contemporaneous Israeli [[Qesem cave]],{{efn-num|The dental similarities with Neanderthals are also present in contemporaneous North African Middle Pleistocene fossils and the later Israeli [[Skhul and Qafzeh hominins]]. So, while Qesem could be a subpopulation of the Neanderthal clade, it is also possible that Qesem instead represents a separate Southwest Asian population. Qesem is also culturally distinct from Europe and Africa, manufacturing the Levantine [[Acheulo-Yabrudian complex]].<ref>{{cite journal|first1=Israel|last1=Hershkovitz|first2=Patricia|last2=Smith|first3=Rachel|last3=Sarig|first4=Rolf|last4=Quam|title=Middle pleistocene dental remains from Qesem Cave (Israel)|journal=American Journal of Physical Anthropology|year=2010 |issn=1096-8644|pages=575–592|volume=144|issue=4|doi=10.1002/ajpa.21446|first5=Laura|last5=Rodríguez|first6=Rebeca|last6=García|first7=Juan Luis|last7=Arsuaga|first8=Ran|last8=Barkai|first9=Avi|last9=Gopher|pmid=21404234 }}</ref>}} which is dentally similar to the Sima de los Huesos hominins.<ref name=CastroPinillos2021/> The timing might coincide with the end of a major glaciation event during Marine Isotope Stage 12 (the [[Elster glaciation|Elster]]/[[Mindel glaciation|Mindel]]/[[Anglian glaciation]]) roughly 450,000 years ago, during the warm interglacial period of [[Marine Isotope Stage 11]].<ref name=Stringer2012/> These "pre-Neanderthals" give way to "early Neanderthals" by the end of Marine Isotope Stage 7 (the [[Penultimate Glacial Period]]). "Early Neanderthals" are differentiated by a combination of both derived and "incipient" Neanderthal traits, and are succeeded by "late" or "classic Neanderthals" by the end of [[Marine Isotope Stage 5e]] (the [[Last Interglacial]]).<ref name=Richards2021>{{cite journal|first1=Gary D.|last1=Richards|first2=Gaspard|last2=Guipert|first3=Rebecca S.|last3=Jabbour|first4=Alban R.|last4=Defleur|title=Neanderthal cranial remains from Baume Moula-Guercy (Soyons, Ardèche, France)|journal=American Journal of Physical Anthropology|year=2021 |issn=1096-8644|pages=203–204|volume=175|issue=1|doi=10.1002/ajpa.24256|pmid=33644865 }}</ref>

==Skeleton==

===Skull===
[[File:Sima de los Huesos Crania.png|thumb|Artistic depiction of the 17 Sima de los Huesos crania]]
====Cranial vault====
The Sima de los Huesos material comprises 17 skulls.{{sfn|Arsuaga|Martı́nez|1997|loc=p. 270}} Compared to Neanderthals, the occipital bone (back of the skull) is less curved, and lacks the characteristic [[occipital bun]]. Like in modern humans and Neanderthals, and unlike in ''H. erectus'', the opisthocranion (the farthest-back point on the skull) is above the superior [[nuchal line]]. The opisthocranion lies at the peak of a flat or slightly convex, semicircular area which extends down to the [[inion]]; the area is dotted with circular pits ("cratered") that became smaller and more dense with age. This area in Neanderthals is characteristically sunken (suprainiac fossa) and smaller; it is a variable trait among Middle Pleistocene specimens. Below this area is a weak occipital torus (a horizontal bulge of bone projecting off the occipital bone) — much weaker than in Neanderthals. The torus is most noticeable near the center of the occipital bone and terminates before reaching the [[asterion (anatomy)|asterion]] (where the occipital bone connects with the [[parietal bone|parietal]] and [[temporal bone]]s). A similar occipital morphology is exhibited in the Swanscombe Skull, but its torus extends farther like in Neanderthals.{{sfn|Arsuaga|Martı́nez|1997|loc=pp. 243–246}}

When the skull is viewed from the back, the sidewalls run parallel to each other and form a shallow [[sagittal keel]] running along the midline of the skull ("house-like" or "en maison" contour) like other European Middle Pleistocene specimens. In contrast, the contour of ''H. erectus'' converges more strongly at the top ("tent-like"), and in Neanderthals it is rounded ("bomb-like" or "en bombe").{{sfn|Arsuaga|Martı́nez|1997|loc=pp. 241–243}} Like in Neanderthals but unlike in many Middle Pleistocene specimens, the supraorbital torus (the [[brow ridge]]) is double-arched instead of forming a single, straight bar. The arches are not divided, but some specimens have a depression on the [[glabella]] (between the brows).<ref name=ArsuagaMartinez2014/>{{sfn|Arsuaga|Martı́nez|1997|loc=p. 261}} When viewed from the top, the skull projects farthest around the glabella.{{sfn|Arsuaga|Martı́nez|1997|loc=p. 263}}

====Brain====
The average brain volume for the 15 Sima de los Huesos skulls for which the metric is calculable is {{cvt|1241|cc}}, ranging from {{cvt|1057|–|1436|cc}}. The average is comparable to other Middle Pleistocene non-''erectus'' specimens which are known to range from {{cvt|1165–1325|cc}}, and on the lower end of the range of variation for Neanderthals which are known to range from {{cvt|1172–1740|cc}}.<ref name=ReyRobles2019/>

Like other archaic humans, the [[parietal lobe]] was proportionally smaller than in modern humans. Compared to Neanderthals, the Sima de los Huesos brain was generally broader (especially towards the back, though this probably does not relate to function). The encephalic rostrum (the frontmost part of the [[corpus callosum]]) was more expanded than in ''H. erectus'' but thinner and narrower than Neanderthals. In Neanderthals and modern humans, typically the [[left hemisphere]] is bigger than the right, related to an expanded [[Broca's area]] associated with language acquisition; in the Sima de los Huesos hominins, brain asymmetry is variable. Like in Neanderthals, the [[temporal lobe]] (associated with visual and [[olfactory memory]]) is narrow. The [[occipital lobe]] (the [[visual cortex]]) is more expanded than in modern humans but much smaller than in Neanderthals.<ref name=ReyRobles2019>{{cite journal|first1=Eva María|last1=Poza-Rey|first2=Aida|last2=Gómez-Robles|first3=Juan Luis|last3=Arsuaga|title=Brain size and organization in the Middle Pleistocene hominins from Sima de los Huesos. Inferences from endocranial variation|journal=Journal of Human Evolution|year=2019|issn=0047-2484|pages=83–87|volume=129|doi=10.1016/j.jhevol.2019.01.006|pmid=30904042 |bibcode=2019JHumE.129...67P |url=https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10070335/ }}</ref>

====Face====
The mid-face (the nose and above) exhibits developed [[prognathism]] (it juts out), to a similar degree as other Middle Pleistocene specimens but not as much as Neanderthals. The face and nose are much wider than in Neanderthals and the cheeks are higher.{{sfn|Arsuaga|Martı́nez|1997|loc=pp. 251–252}} Like in Neanderthals and most modern humans but unlike ''H. erectus'', the bottom rim of the [[piriform aperture]] (nose hole) is raised. Like in Neanderthals (though to a lesser degree), the [[anterior nasal spine]] and [[inferior nasal concha]] at the base of the piriform aperature are fused, and the [[lacrimal groove|lateral crests]] are so well defined that they extend all the way to and connect with the nasal spine/concha. Unlike in Neanderthals, the floor of the [[nasal cavity]] is flat instead of sloping down.{{sfn|Arsuaga|Martı́nez|1997|loc=pp. 268–269}} 

[[File:AT1.png|thumb|AT1 jawbone]]
The dental and jaw anatomy is generally Neanderthal-like, and similarly the regions of the temporal bone that are functionally relevant to chewing align closely with Neanderthals (the other regions are more basal). The tooth rows are square-shaped, like in Petralona 1, and in some Neanderthals.<ref name=ArsuagaMartinez2014/> The mandible is mostly like that of Neanderthals but has multiple [[mental foramen|mental foramina]], a high [[mylohyoid line]] at the level of the third molar, and a more vertical and developed chin.<ref name=QuamMartinez2024/> The presumably female jaws are much smaller and have smoother muscle attachments, especially at the [[angle of the mandible|gonoid]] and [[coronoid process of the mandible]]. This degree of [[sexual dimorphism]] is notably larger than in modern humans.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=Antonio|last1=Rosas|first2=Markus|last2=Bastir|first3=Cayetana|last3=Martı́nez-Maza|first4=Jose Marı́a|last4=Bermúdez de Castro|title=Sexual dimorphism in the Atapuerca-SH hominids: the evidence from the mandibles|journal=Journal of Human Evolution|year= 2002|issn=0047-2484|pages=451–474|volume=42|issue=4|doi=10.1006/jhev.2001.0536|pmid=11908956 |bibcode=2002JHumE..42..451R }}</ref><ref name=ArsuagaMartinez2014/>

The upper teeth are Neanderthal-like, with large and strongly [[shovel-shaped incisors]] and canines, as well as [[taurodontism]] in the [[molar (tooth)|molars]]. Tubercles are infrequently found on the incisors, canines, and molars (the [[cusp of Carabelli]]); tubercles are far more common on Neanderthal teeth.<ref name=CastroPinillos2021/> The back teeth are notably smaller and less complex than in most other archaic humans, more similar to recent humans.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=María|last1=Martinón-Torres|first2=Petra|last2=Spěváčková|first3=Ana|last3=Gracia-Téllez|first4=Ignacio|last4=Martínez|title=Morphometric analysis of molars in a Middle Pleistocene population shows a mosaic of 'modern' and Neanderthal features|journal=Journal of Anatomy|year=2013|issn=1469-7580|pages=353–363|volume=223|issue=4|pmid=23914934|pmc=3791128|doi=10.1111/joa.12090|first5=Emiliano|last5=Bruner|first6=Juan Luis|last6=Arsuaga|first7=José María|last7=Bermúdez de Castro}}</ref><ref name=CastroPinillos2021/> The incisors and canines of the lower teeth exhibit somewhat weaker shoveling than in Neanderthals. The morphology of the lower [[premolar]]s and molars are Neanderthal-like, though there is a greater range of variation in [[cusp (tooth)|cusp]] size and shape.<ref name=CastroPinillos2021>{{cite journal|first1=José María|last1=Bermúdez de Castro|first2=Marina|last2=Martínez de Pinillos|first3=Laura|last3=Martín-Francés|first4=Mario|last4=Modesto-Mata|title=Dental remains of the Middle Pleistocene hominins from the Sima de los Huesos site (Sierra de Atapuerca, Spain): Mandibular dentition|journal=The Anatomical Record|year=2021 |issn=1932-8494|pages=2405–2407|volume=307|issue=7|doi=10.1002/ar.24840|first5=Cecilia|last5=García-Campos|first6=Juan Luis|last6=Arsuaga|first7=María|last7=Martinón-Torres|pmid=34851548 }}</ref>

===Size===
The Sima de los Huesos hominins, like other archaic populations, seem to have had much heavier skeletons than modern humans, which presumably supported greater muscle mass and equated to an overall heavier build. The skeletal weight of the Sima de los Huesos hominins may have been roughly 36% greater than that of modern humans.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=José-Miguel|last1=Carretero|first2=Laura|last2=Rodríguez|first3=Rebeca|last3=García-González|first4=Rolf-Michael|last4=Quam|title=Exploring bone volume and skeletal weight in the Middle Pleistocene humans from the Sima de los Huesos site (Sierra de Atapuerca, Spain)|journal=Journal of Anatomy|year=2018|issn=0021-8782|pages=740–754|volume=233|issue=6|pmid=30280382|pmc=6231173|doi=10.1111/joa.12886|first5=Juan-Luis|last5=Arsuaga}}</ref>

Based on 19 complete male and 5 complete female [[long bone]]s (sex assignment based on the size of the bone), average adult height was rather tall for archaic humans — respectively {{cvt|169.5|and|157.7|cm|ftin|0}}.<ref name=ArsuagaCarretero2015/> Sexing the [[femur|femora]] based on anatomical landmarks reassigns some of the assumed-male femora to female, with one potentially female femur (FXIII) belonging to someone possibly reaching {{cvt|88|kg}}. In general, large female body size may not have been uncommon in archaic humans.<ref name=CarreteroRodriguez2024/>

The body mass of the complete male Pelvis 1 ("Elvis") may have belonged to someone {{cvt|90.3|to|92.5|kg}} in weight,<ref name=ArsuagaCarretero2015>{{cite journal|first1=Juan Luis|last1=Arsuaga|first2=José-Miguel|last2=Carretero|first3=Carlos|last3=Lorenzo|first4=Asier|last4=Gómez-Olivencia|title=Postcranial morphology of the middle Pleistocene humans from Sima de los Huesos, Spain|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|year=2015|pages=11524–11529|volume=112|issue=37|pmid=26324920|pmc=4577189|doi=10.1073/pnas.1514828112|first5=Adrián|last5=Pablos|first6=Laura|last6=Rodríguez|first7=Rebeca|last7=García-González|first8=Alejandro|last8=Bonmatí|first9=Rolf M.|last9=Quam|first10=Ana|last10=Pantoja-Pérez|first11=Ignacio|last11=Martínez|first12=Arantza|last12=Aranburu|first13=Ana|last13=Gracia-Téllez|first14=Eva|last14=Poza-Rey|first15=Nohemi|last15=Sala|first16=Nuria|last16=García|first17=Almudena|last17=Alcázar de Velasco|first18=Gloria|last18=Cuenca-Bescós|first19=José María|last19=Bermúdez de Castro|first20=Eudald|last20=Carbonell|doi-access=free |bibcode=2015PNAS..11211524A }}</ref> potentially up to {{cvt|100|kg}}.<ref name=CarreteroRodriguez2024/> "Elvis" has one of the highest weight estimates of an archaic human.<ref name=CarreteroRodriguez2012/>

Based on the [[tarsus (skeleton)|tarsus]], average height was about {{cvt|174|cm|ftin}} for males and {{cvt|162|cm|ftin}} for females, with an average weight of {{cvt|70|kg}}. The highest weight estimate is {{cvt|89.2–92.2|kg}}, similar to "Elvis".<ref name=PablosArsuaga2024/> Based on the [[metatarsal]]s and [[phalanx bone|phalanges]], average size was {{cvt|175|and|174|cm|ftin}} and {{cvt|80|and|77|kg}} for males and females, respectively.<ref name=PablosArsuaga2024b/>

In general, Middle Pleistocene height estimates range from {{cvt|165|to|170|cm|ftin}} — though there are a few taller individuals — and Neanderthals were slightly shorter on average.<ref name=CarreteroRodriguez2012>{{cite journal|first1=José-Miguel|last1=Carretero|first2=Laura|last2=Rodríguez|first3=Rebeca|last3=García-González|first4=Juan-Luis|last4=Arsuaga|title=Stature estimation from complete long bones in the Middle Pleistocene humans from the Sima de los Huesos, Sierra de Atapuerca (Spain)|journal=Journal of Human Evolution|year=2012|issn=0047-2484|pages=242–255|volume=62|issue=2|doi=10.1016/j.jhevol.2011.11.004|first5=Asier|last5=Gómez-Olivencia|first6=Carlos|last6=Lorenzo|first7=Alejandro|last7=Bonmatí|first8=Ana|last8=Gracia|first9=Ignacio|last9=Martínez|first10=Rolf|last10=Quam|pmid=22196156 |bibcode=2012JHumE..62..242C |url=https://eprints.ucm.es/26998/1/1-s2.0-S0047248411002193-_01.pdf }}</ref>

===Postcranium===
Before the discovery of the Sima de los Huesos hominins, the characterization of the Early and Middle Pleistocene human body plan was based almost exclusively on the Kenyan [[Turkana Boy]]. This specimen was originally reconstructed to resemble the narrower modern human body plan rather than the stockier Neanderthal body plan (which has since been called into question with more fossil discoveries), implying that the Neanderthal body plan was a unique adaptation — presumably as a response to cold climates. Every bone in the human skeleton is represented by the Sima de los Huesos material, and postcranial remains make up about half of the material.<ref name=ArsuagaCarretero2015/>

====Torso====
The rib material is largely fragmented, with only a complete 1st, 11th, and 12th rib identified. Because the 1st rib is thicker dorsoventrally (front-to-back), and the pelvis is bigger anteroposteriorly (front-to-back) and mediolaterally (left-to-right) than in both modern humans and Neanderthals, the Sima de los Huesos hominins may have had an expanded [[thorax]] (chest) like in Neanderthals. The wide thorax and pelvis may be the ancestral condition for humans, with the narrow form of modern humans evolving more recently, but this is difficult to test given the paucity of postcranial remains predating the Late Pleistocene.<ref name=ArsuagaCarretero2015/><ref name=OlivenciaArsuaga2024/>

[[File:Pelvis masculina (Elvis). Sima de los Huesos.jpg|thumb|"Elvis" the pelvis]]
The [[pelvic cavity]] of "Elvis" (a male) is so wide that a modern human baby would be able to pass through it; and a female's would have been even wider. This could indicate the Sima de los Huesos hominins were born with a bigger head and brain volume. A broad pelvis would impede [[abduction (anatomy)|abduction]] at the hip joint, and was compensated by flaring [[iliac crest]]s and a long [[femoral neck]].<ref>{{cite journal|first1=Juan-Luis|last1=Arsuaga|first2=Carlos|last2=Lorenzo|first3=José-Miguel|last3=Carretero|first4=Ana|last4=Gracia|title=A complete human pelvis from the Middle Pleistocene of Spain|journal=Nature|year=1999|issn=1476-4687|pages=255–258|volume=399|issue=6733|doi=10.1038/20430|first5=Ignacio|last5=Martínez|first6=Nuria|last6=García|first7=José-María Bermúdez de|last7=Castro|first8=Eudald|last8=Carbonell|pmid=10353247 |bibcode=1999Natur.399..255A }}</ref> Still, this would have made movement much more energetically expensive, especially over long distances, compared to modern humans.<ref name=CarreteroRodriguez2012/>

Like in Neanderthals, the [[atlas (bone)|atlas]] (first [[cervical vertebrae|neck vertebra]]) is wide dorsoventrally (probably related to the large [[foramen magnum]], where the spine connects into the skull), and the [[axis (bone)|axis]] is craniocadually (top-to-bottom) shortened. The [[atlanto-axial joint]] (between the atlas and axis, important in rotating the neck) is mediolaterally expanded.<ref name=ArsuagaCarretero2015/><ref>{{cite journal|first1=Asier|last1=Gómez-Olivencia|first2=José Miguel|last2=Carretero|first3=Juan Luis|last3=Arsuaga|first4=Laura|last4=Rodríguez-García|title=Metric and morphological study of the upper cervical spine from the Sima de los Huesos site (Sierra de Atapuerca, Burgos, Spain)|journal=Journal of Human Evolution|date=1 July 2007|issn=0047-2484|pages=19–23|volume=53|issue=1|doi=10.1016/j.jhevol.2006.12.006|first5=Rebeca|last5=García-González|first6=Ignacio|last6=Martínez|pmid=17467038 |bibcode=2007JHumE..53....6G |url=https://eprints.ucm.es/id/eprint/26867/1/1-s2.0-S0047248407000565_01.pdf }}</ref>  Like other archaic humans, the spinous process (jutting straight out of the vertebra) of the 6th and 7th neck vertebrae are long and horizontal — although it is shorter and more inclined than in Neanderthals.<ref name=ArsuagaCarretero2015/> The shorter and more stabilized neck of Neanderthals and the Sima de los Huesos hominins could be related to balance with the broad chest and pelvis; the [[semicircular canals]] in the [[bony labyrinth|inner ear]] (which affect balance) are similar to those of Neanderthals, but the posterior canal is lower and the anterior canal does not exhibit the same degree of torsion. The differences, if functional, could be related to the larger average body size of the Sima de los Huesos hominins.<ref name=VelezQuam2023/>

Like in Neanderthals, the [[lumbar vertebrae]] (lower spine) exhibit less curvature ([[lordosis#Lumbar hypolordosis|hypolordosis]], "flatback") than in modern humans. Like in modern humans, Turkana Boy, and the [[australopithecine]] ''[[Paranthropus robustus]]'', the transverse processes jut out of the vertebra dorsolaterally (from the sides angled back), whereas the dorsal (back) orientation is not seen in Neanderthals.<ref name=ArsuagaCarretero2015/><ref name=OlivenciaArsuaga2024>{{cite journal|first1=Asier|last1=Gómez-Olivencia|first2=Juan Luis|last2=Arsuaga|title=The Sima de los Huesos thorax and lumbar spine: Selected traits and state-of-the-art|journal=The Anatomical Record|year=2024 |issn=1932-8494|pages=2483–2487|volume=307|issue=7|doi=10.1002/ar.25414|pmid=38450997 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

====Limbs====
Like in Neanderthals, there is a [[sulcus (morphology)|sulcus]] (groove) on the dorsal side of the axillary border of almost all of the [[shoulder blade]]s (by the armpit), as opposed to the ventral sulcus of any other hominin specimen. This could have functional implications for the mobility and structure of the [[shoulder joint]].<ref>{{cite journal|first1=Rebeca|last1=García-González|first2=Laura|last2=Rodríguez|first3=Azahara|last3=Salazar-Fernández|first4=Juan Luis|last4=Arsuaga|title=Updated study of adult and subadult pectoral girdle bones from Sima de los Huesos site (Sierra de Atapuerca, Burgos, Spain). Anatomical and age estimation keys|journal=The Anatomical Record|year=2023 |issn=1932-8494|pages=2512–2514|volume=307|issue=7|doi=10.1002/ar.25158|first5=José-Miguel|last5=Carretero|pmid=36656646 }}</ref> The [[glenoid fossa]] (where the shoulder blade connects with the [[humerus]]) is taller and narrower compared to modern humans. Like in Neanderthals, the head of the humerus has an oval cross-section, the [[lesser tubercle]] is bigger, the [[deltoid tuberosity]] is narrower, the bone of the [[diaphysis|shaft]] is thicker, and the [[olecranon fossa]] (which connects with the [[ulna]]) is broader and deeper.<ref name=ArsuagaCarretero2015/> The ulna and [[radius (bone)|radius]] are usually also characteristically Neanderthal, lending greater mechanical advantage in rotating the forearm, but some can fall instead within the range of variation of modern humans — implying Neanderthals lost some variability here. The forearm is also longer than in Neanderthals. The hand is well-adapted for mobility and a precision grip, like in Neanderthals and modern humans.<ref name=ArsuagaCarretero2015/><ref>{{cite journal|first1=Laura|last1=Rodríguez|first2=Rebeca|last2=García-González|first3=Juan Luis|last3=Arsuaga|first4=José-Miguel|last4=Carretero|title=Uncovering the adult morphology of the forearm bones from the Sima de los Huesos Site in Atapuerca (Spain), with comments on biomechanical features|journal=The Anatomical Record|year=2023 |issn=1932-8494|pages=2570–2571|volume=307|issue=7|doi=10.1002/ar.25281|pmid=37345623 |hdl=10612/16850|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

Like other archaic humans, the femur has a flattened neck, the shaft is mediolaterally expanded near the top, the neck-to-shaft angle is low, the [[gluteal tuberosity]] is large, there is not a true [[pilaster]] (a vertical ridge unique to modern humans), and the bone is thicker.<ref name=ArsuagaCarretero2015/> These differences may be related to supporting the heavier and more robust archaic skeleton, and compensating for the broad pelvis. Like in Neanderthals, the [[patella]] (knee bone) has deeper [[joint|articular]] (jointing) surfaces, which could be related to stability.<ref name=CarreteroRodriguez2024>{{cite journal|first1=José-Miguel|last1=Carretero|first2=Laura|last2=Rodríguez|first3=Rebeca|last3=García-González|first4=Juan-Luis|last4=Arsuaga|title=Main morphological characteristics and sexual dimorphism of hominin adult femora from the Sima de los Huesos Middle Pleistocene site (Sierra de Atapuerca, Spain)|journal=The Anatomical Record|year=2024 |issn=1932-8494|pages=2590–2599|volume=307|issue=7|doi=10.1002/ar.25331|doi-access=free|pmid=37794824 |hdl=10259/9329|hdl-access=free}}</ref> Like in Neanderthals, the articular surfaces of the [[tibia]] are flat, and the proximal [[epiphysis]] (at the knee-end) has a large retroversion angle (rotated backwards) which would have stabilized the knee joint during bouts of intense activity. Habitual squatting is evidenced by [[hypertrophy]] (enlargement) of the medial malleolus (the ankle bone that connects to the tibia) and wearing near the ankle on about a quarter of the tibiae.<ref name=ArsuagaCarretero2015/><ref name=RodriguezGonzalez2023/> The tibial pilaster is robust, which is only seen in the 400,000 year old English [[Boxgrove Man]]. Compared to Neanderthals, the tibiae are proportionally longer, more similar to modern humans. Longer legs would mean they were more energetically efficient while walking than Neanderthals, but the [[quadriceps]] muscle had less [[mechanical advantage]]. Like in Neanderthals, the tibial shaft is ellipsoid, as opposed to the triangular shaft of modern humans, Boxgrove Man, and [[Kabwe 1]]. The [[fibula]] indicates the [[gastrocnemius]] and [[soleus muscle]]s were shorter than in modern humans, indicating higher energy costs while moving.<ref name=RodriguezGonzalez2023>{{cite journal|first1=Laura|last1=Rodríguez|first2=Rebeca|last2=García-González|first3=Juan Luis|last3=Arsuaga|first4=José-Miguel|last4=Carretero|title=Exploring the morphology of adult tibia and fibula from Sima de los Huesos site in sierra de Atapuerca, Burgos, Spain|journal=The Anatomical Record|year=2023 |issn=1932-8494|pages=2620–2631|volume=307|issue=7|doi=10.1002/ar.25336|doi-access=free|pmid=37792425 |hdl=10259/9328|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

Like other archaic humans, the [[body of talus|trochlea]] (in the ankle) is tall, broad, and rectangular (as opposed to the wedge-shaped one of modern humans), but the head is narrower than in Neanderthals and modern humans. The shape of the trochlea may have improved [[anatomical terms of motion#Flexion and extension of the foot|dorsiflexion and plantarflexion]] (up and down motion) in the ankle.<ref name=ArsuagaCarretero2015/><ref name=PablosArsuaga2024>{{cite journal|first1=Adrián|last1=Pablos|first2=Juan Luis|last2=Arsuaga|title=Tarsals from the Sima de los Huesos Middle Pleistocene site (Atapuerca, Burgos, Spain)|journal=The Anatomical Record|year=2024 |issn=1932-8494|pages=2659–2660|volume=307|issue=7|doi=10.1002/ar.25425|pmid=38477186 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Nonetheless, like in Neanderthals, the smaller malleolar fossa (which connects to the malleolus) on the fibula indicates a narrower range of dorsiflexion than in modern humans,<ref name=RodriguezGonzalez2023/> though it does stabilize the ankle better.<ref name=PablosArsuaga2024/> Like in Neanderthals, the [[calcaneum|heel bone]] is long, which may have improved shock absorption to compensate for the larger build. The Sima de los Huesos hominins were probably bigger than Neanderthals, and similarly the sustentaculum talus (which supports the [[plantar calcaneonavicular ligament|spring ligament]]) projects even farther out than in Neanderthals.<ref name=PablosArsuaga2024/><ref name=ArsuagaCarretero2015/> Like in Neanderthals, the phalanges as well as metatarsals 3–5 have a broad base, and the [[big toe]] is wider.<ref name=ArsuagaCarretero2015/> The metatarsals and phalanges, in general, are much broader and more robust than in Neanderthals, which may be related to their bigger size. They probably walked and ran with the forefoot striking the ground first.<ref name=PablosArsuaga2024b>{{cite journal|first1=Adrián|last1=Pablos|first2=Juan Luis|last2=Arsuaga|title=Metatarsals and foot phalanges from the Sima de los Huesos Middle Pleistocene site (Atapuerca, Burgos, Spain)|journal=The Anatomical Record|year=2024 |issn=1932-8494|pages=2696–2707|volume=307|issue=7|doi=10.1002/ar.25412|pmid=38380556 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Pathology==
===Diseases===
[[File:Miguelon - MCN 4149 (cropped).jpg|thumb|left|upright=0.8|Cranium 5 ("[[Miguelón]]") presents severe tooth decay.<ref name=AscasoAdiego2016/>]]
Cranium 5 presents severe dental decay, moderate [[gum disease]], and [[alveolar osteitis]] on the left side. All of the teeth exhibit excessive wearing. There is extensive [[bone destruction patterns in periodontal disease|alveolar bone loss]], causing [[overeruption]] of the teeth; at least a third of the root of every tooth is exposed. This individual seems to have been treating his gum disease with a [[toothpick]], and similar toothpick grooves are found in some isolated teeth in the Sima de los Huesos. The lower left third molar (M<sub>3</sub>) exhibits chipping. The upper left first premolar (P<sup>3</sup>) was badly chipped in life, exposing the [[pulp cavity]]. The wound appears to have suffered from chronic infection, leading to [[periapical cyst]] and [[fistula]] formation with remodeling of the surrounding bone. The lower left incisors also formed cysts, with pulp cavity exposure likely stemming from excessive loading and wearing in life; the upper incisors are similarly heavily ground down. The infection seems to have progressed to [[orbital cellulitis]] in the eye, and may have eventually progressed to [[sepsis]], leading to death.<ref name=AscasoAdiego2016>{{cite journal|last1=Ascaso |first1=F. |last2=Adiego |first2=M.I. |year=2016 |title=''Homo heidelbergensis'': the oldest case of odontogenic orbital cellulitis? |journal=Acta Ophthalmologica |volume=94 |doi=10.1111/j.1755-3768.2016.0022 |issn=1755-375X|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|year=2013 |title=Orofacial pathology in ''Homo heidelbergensis'': The case of Skull 5 from the Sima de los Huesos site (Atapuerca, Spain) |journal=Quaternary International |volume=295 |pages=83–93 |doi=10.1016/j.quaint.2012.02.005 |issn=1040-6182 |last1=Gracia-Téllez |first1=Ana |last2=Arsuaga |first2=Juan-Luis |last3=Martínez |first3=Ignacio |last4=Martín-Francés |first4=Laura |last5=Martinón-Torres |first5=María |last6=Bermúdez De Castro |first6=José-María |last7=Bonmatí |first7=Alejandro |last8=Lira |first8=Jaime |bibcode=2013QuInt.295...83G}}</ref>

About 40% of the teeth exhibit [[enamel hypoplasia]] resulting from bouts of nutritional stress, peaking at about 3½ years of age. This could indicate the weaning age, which was probably around 4 years of age in Neanderthals, like recent hunter gatherers. Neanderthals suffered even higher rates and more intense bouts of hypoplasia, either because their subsistence strategies were less efficient, or because they lived in harsher environments.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=J. M. |last1=Bermúdez de Castro |first2=P. J. |last2=Pérez |year=1995 |title=Enamel Hypoplasia in the Middle Pleistocene Hominids From Atapuerca (Spain) |journal=[[American Journal of Physical Anthropology]] |volume=96 |issue=3 |pages=301–314 |doi=10.1002/ajpa.1330960307 |pmid=7785727}}</ref>

"Elvis", based on joint degeneration, may have lived for more than 45 years. He presented: lumbar [[kyphosis]] (excessive curving of the lumbar vertebrae in the lower back), L5–S1 [[spondylolisthesis]] (misalignment of the last lumbar vertebra with the first [[sacral vertebra]]), and [[Baastrup disease]] on L4 and 5 (enlargement of the spinous processes). These would have caused lower back pain, significantly limiting movement, and may indicate group care.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=A. |last1=Bonmatí |first2=A. |last2=Gómez-Olivencia |first3=J. L. |last3=Arsuaga |author-link3=Juan Luis Arsuaga |display-authors=et al. |year=2010 |title=Middle Pleistocene lower back and pelvis from an aged human individual from the Sima de los Huesos site, Spain |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=107 |issue=43 |pages=18386–18391 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1012131107 |pmc=2973007 |pmid=20937858 |bibcode=2010PNAS..10718386B |doi-access=free}}</ref>

The adolescent Cranium 14 was diagnosed with lambdoid single suture [[craniosynostosis]] (immature closing of the left [[lambdoid suture]] leading to skull deformities as development continued). This is a rare condition in modern humans, occurring in less than 6 out of every 200,000 individuals. The individual died around the age of 10, suggesting it was not abandoned due to its deformity as has been done in historical times, and received the same quality of care as any other child.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=A. |last1=Garcia |first2=J. L. |last2=Arsuaga |author-link2=Juan Luis Arsuaga |first3=I. |last3=Martínez |display-authors=et al. |year=2009 |title=Craniosynostosis in the Middle Pleistocene human Cranium 14 from the Sima de los Huesos, Atapuerca, Spain |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=106 |issue=16 |pages=6573–6578 |doi=10.1073/pnas.0900965106 |pmc=2672549 |pmid=19332773 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

===Hibernation===
The adolescents, especially, present pathologies consistent with chronic metabolic and malnutritional diseases, which could be consistent with insufficient fat reserves during [[hibernation]]. The adults do not seem to have suffered to the same degree. Hibernation can be induced in modern humans with injection of [[cyclic adenosine monophosphate|5′-AMP]] (a [[secondary messenger]]) which in hibernating animals is normally produced by [[brown adipose tissue]].<ref name=BartsiokasArsuaga2020>{{cite journal|first1=Antonis|last1=Bartsiokas|first2=Juan-Luis|last2=Arsuaga|title=Hibernation in hominins from Atapuerca, Spain half a million years ago|journal=L'Anthropologie|year=2020|issn=0003-5521|article-number=102797|volume=124|series=PaléoanthropologieGéochronologie|issue=5|doi=10.1016/j.anthro.2020.102797}}</ref>{{efn-num|There are vague historical references to hibernation in humans, such as the ostensible six-month uninterrupted sleep "Lotska" by peasants in [[Pskov]], Russia, during the winter; or [[Herodotus]]' report of people north of [[Scythia]] (i.e., Russia) sleeping for half the year.<ref name=BartsiokasArsuaga2020/>}}

The Sima de los Huesos fossils bear several signs of [[chronic kidney disease–mineral and bone disorder]] (CKD–MBD), indicated by frequent [[osteitis fibrosa]] and [[renal osteodystrophy]] (ROD). They similarly present signs of [[vitamin D deficiency]] (which proceeds from CKD), and resultant [[hypocalcemia]] and [[secondary hyperparathyroidism]] (2HPT).<ref name=BartsiokasArsuaga2020/> These diseases are exhibited altogether in hibernating animals with insufficient fat stores. Fat deficiency leads to the arrestment of [[lipolysis]], preventing the release of vitamin D stored in the fat cells. It also boosts [[cortisol]] levels to aid fat [[catabolism]] at the expense of serum calcium levels; [[hypercortisolism]] ultimately progresses to kidney disease. Fat deficiency is a major source of hibernation mortality.<ref name=BartsiokasArsuaga2020/>

The relevant pathologies are as follows:<ref name=BartsiokasArsuaga2020/>
*Regular bouts of extreme vitamin D deficiency cyclically caused lines of arrested growth in the bone, consistent with acquired [[rickets]] (rachitic osteoplaques). The [[puberty|pubescent]] Cranium 9 presents four such osteoplaques of rachitic [[hyperostosis]] —  four short adolescent growth spurts separated by arrested growth ([[dormancy]]), a pattern characteristic of arousal from [[torpor]]. In other words, this individual may have roused from hibernation four times in a probably four-month hibernation period.
*"Elvis" presents several [[brown tumor]]s (a type of osteitis fibrosa), part of the recovery process from severe CKD–MBD, rickets, and 2HPT.
*Some fossils show calcification of soft tissue, consistent with [[calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystal deposition disease]]. In bats, this is caused by increased production of [[adenosine triphosphate]] (ATP) during lipolysis of brown adipose tissue, to produce heat during bouts of arousal from hibernation.
*The entire population seems to have regularly suffered from [[periosteal reaction|subperiosteal new bone growth]] and consequent [[bone resorption]] in many places (especially the phalanges as well as the [[lamina dura]] in the teeth), resulting from severe rickets, 2HPT, and [[osteomalacia]] as a consequence of ROD during the healing process.
*Some ribs present the [[rachitic rosary]] (bead-like growths near the [[sternum]]) stemming from renal rickets and 2HPT.

Like the cave bears at the site, the Sima de los Huesos hominins may have developed hibernation to cope with the frigid and lean winters. Similarly, one adolescent cave bear specimen from the Sima de los Huesos presents subperiosteal new bone growth resulting from rickets. The age demographic of the Sima de los Huesos hominins is skewed towards adolescents, which is also observed in hibernation-related mortality events. Hibernation does not seem to have been practiced by Neanderthals, possibly because they were metabolically better at withstanding the cold and were more efficient hunters capable of sustaining themselves year-round.<ref name=BartsiokasArsuaga2020/>

===Violence===
Crania 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 14, and 17 display several perimortem fractures (injured around the time of death). These fractures may have originated while falling down the shaft — not necessarily while they were alive but at least near the time of death. Only 4% of the long bone material presents perimortem fracturing,<ref name=SalaPerez2016>{{cite journal|first1=Nohemi|last1=Sala|first2=Ana|last2=Pantoja-Pérez|first3=Juan Luis|last3=Arsuaga|first4=Adrián|last4=Pablos|title=The Sima de los Huesos Crania: Analysis of the cranial breakage patterns|journal=Journal of Archaeological Science|year=2016|issn=0305-4403|pages=36–43|volume=72|doi=10.1016/j.jas.2016.06.001|first5=Ignacio|last5=Martínez|bibcode=2016JArSc..72...25S }}</ref> and they lack any major injuries. American archeologist [[Erik Trinkaus]] noticed a similar pattern in Neanderthals, and suggested individuals who could not walk or keep up with a group while moving between cave sites were left behind. If true, then only individuals without major trauma to the lower limbs would be found at cave sites ([[survivor bias]]). It is unclear if this can be applied here.<ref name=SalaMartinez2024/> The only pathological foot specimen is a fourth metatarsal (AT-534) which presents a [[periosteal reaction]] to presumably a [[march fracture]], a minor injury common in [[barefoot running|barefoot runners]].<ref name=PablosArsuaga2024b/>

[[File:Sima de los Huesos - Cranium 17.png|thumb|Cranium 17 with two identical fractures in the forehead]]
Cranium 17 presents two nearly identical, connected, rectangular perimortem depression fractures on the left [[squamous part of the frontal bone|frontal squama]] (Trauma 1 below and Trauma 2 above). The injuries are angled in [[acute angle|acutely]] at different trajectories, respectively 32.5°–44.8° and 49.2°. The injuries are consistent with powerful blunt force trauma, passing through the bone into the brain. The identical shape (even baring the same notch in the same position) suggests that they were caused by the same object, and their different trajectories suggests that they were caused by two separate actions; so it is improbable this individual got these fractures from simply falling into the Sima de los Huesos, or being struck by randomly falling limestone blocks. They may be the result of an intentional attack by another human with a tool in the right hand, resulting in her death.<ref name=SalaArsuaga2015/>

Similarly, there is evidence that the Sima de los Huesos hominins were predominantly [[handedness|right-handed]];<ref name=LozanoMosquera2009/><ref name=SalaArsuaga2015/> and in [[forensic medicine]], multiple blows to the face above the [[hat brim]] is normally interpreted as an assault ("hat brim rule"). This further means that the individual represented by Cranium 17 was already dead before dropping into the Sima de los Huesos, and — lacking any carnivore damage — was most likely interred by other humans.<ref name=SalaArsuaga2015/> The perimortem fracturing on Cranium 5 on the frontal and left parietal, as well as Cranium 11 on the left parietal, may have also originated from interpersonal violence.<ref name=SalaPerez2016/> No defensive injuries on the arms have been discovered.<ref name=SalaMartinez2024/>

Interpersonal violence in the fossil record is difficult to demonstrate. {{As of|2015}}, the only other specimens that bear some strong evidence of this in the human fossil record is the Neanderthal [[Shanidar Cave|Shanidar 3]] and the modern human [[Sungir|Sunghir 1]].<ref name=SalaArsuaga2015>{{cite journal|first1=Nohemi|last1=Sala|first2=Juan Luis|last2=Arsuaga|first3=Ana|last3=Pantoja-Pérez|first4=Adrián|last4=Pablos|title=Lethal Interpersonal Violence in the Middle Pleistocene|journal=PLOS ONE|year=2015|issn=1932-6203|article-number=e0126589|volume=10|issue=5|pmid=26018668|pmc=4446311|doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589|doi-access=free|first5=Ignacio|last5=Martínez|first6=Rolf M.|last6=Quam|first7=Asier|last7=Gómez-Olivencia|first8=José María Bermúdez de|last8=Castro|first9=Eudald|last9=Carbonell|bibcode=2015PLoSO..1026589S }}</ref>

==Culture==
===Paleoenvironment===
[[File:Atapuerca carnivore skull 3.jpg|thumb|left|''[[Ursus deningeri]]'' skull from the Sima de los Huesos]]
The Sima de los Huesos hominins were associated with an unusually diverse carnivore assemblage: the cave bear ''U. deningeri'' (this population seems to have been mostly herbivorous), wolf (possibly ''[[Canis mosbachensis]]''), the [[red fox]], the cave lion ''[[Panthera fossilis]]'', the [[European jaguar]], the [[cave lynx]], the [[pine marten]], the [[least weasel]], the [[European polecat]], and the [[European badger]]. This may indicate a [[productivity (ecology)|high-productivity]] ecosystem.<ref name=GarciaFeranec2009/><ref>{{cite journal|first1=Nuria|last1=García|first2=Israel Jesus|last2=Jimenez|first3=Raquel|last3=Blázquez-Orta|first4=Juan Luis|last4=Arsuaga|title=Updates to the carnivore fauna from the Sima de los Huesos|journal=The Anatomical Record|year=2024 |issn=1932-8494|pages=2246–2258|volume=307|issue=7|doi=10.1002/ar.25199|pmid=36929694 }}</ref> [[Rodent]]s and other small mammals are far less common, and large herbivores are absent, consistent with the characterization of the site as a natural pitfall trap. The [[cave hyena]], which is a common occurrence in similarly aged sites across Europe, is mysteriously absent; it is possible that the Sima de los Huesos hominins were [[competitive exclusion principle|outcompeting]] them in the region.<ref name=GarciaFeranec2009>{{cite journal|first1=N.|last1=García García|first2=R. S.|last2=Feranec|first3=J. L.|last3=Arsuaga|first4=J. M.|last4=Bermúdez de Castro|title=Isotopic analysis of the ecology of herbivores and carnivores from the Middle Pleistocene deposits of the Sierra De Atapuerca, northern Spain|journal=Journal of Archaeological Science|year= 2009|issn=0305-4403|pages=1142–1151|volume=36|issue=5|doi=10.1016/j.jas.2008.12.018|first5=E.|last5=Carbonell|bibcode=2009JArSc..36.1142G |url=https://eprints.ucm.es/27149/1/1-s2.0-S0305440308003269-main_01.pdf }}</ref><ref name=GarciaArsuaga2011>{{cite journal|first1=Nuria|last1=García|first2=Juan Luis|last2=Arsuaga|title=The Sima de los Huesos (Burgos, northern Spain): palaeoenvironment and habitats of ''Homo heidelbergensis'' during the Middle Pleistocene|journal=Quaternary Science Reviews|year= 2011|issn=0277-3791|pages=1413–1419|volume=30|series=Early Human Evolution in the Western Palaearctic: Ecological Scenarios|issue=11|doi=10.1016/j.quascirev.2010.11.008|bibcode=2011QSRv...30.1413G }}</ref> At TD10.1, there is evidence of cave lion hunting and butchery; exploitation of carnivores is rare in the Middle Pleistocene, and this may have been a sporadic occurrence.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=Ruth|last1=Blasco|first2=Jordi|last2=Rosell|first3=Juan Luis|last3=Arsuaga|first4=José M.|last4=Bermúdez de Castro|title=The hunted hunter: the capture of a lion (''Panthera leo fossilis'') at the Gran Dolina site, Sierra de Atapuerca, Spain|journal=Journal of Archaeological Science|year=2010|issn=0305-4403|pages=2051–2060|volume=37|issue=8|doi=10.1016/j.jas.2010.03.010|first5=Eudald|last5=Carbonell|bibcode=2010JArSc..37.2051B }}</ref> ''U. deningeri'' is the most common animal at the site but is not found anywhere else in the Sierra de Atapuerca. They may have been especially susceptible to falling into the Sima de los Huesos as they needed to seek out caves to hibernate in annually.<ref name=GarciaArsuaga2011/> Three human ribs exhibit peeling and may have been fed on by a bear that fell in.<ref name=SalaMartinez2024/>

Several well-preserved bat fossils (mostly [[greater mouse-eared bat]] and a few [[Mehely's horseshoe bat]]) as well as significant [[guano]] accumulation were also found, probably representing overwintering roosts. Early Pleistocene deposits seem to indicate bats roosted in the area year-round but only seasonally in the Middle Pleistocene when human activity increased. While the deteriorating climate of the time may have altered roosting behavior, their inability to recover during warmer periods (as other small mammals did) may indicate that they were disturbed by local human activity.<ref name=GalanLahuerta2019>{{cite journal|first1=Julia|last1=Galán|first2=Carmen|last2=Núñez-Lahuerta|first3=Juan Manuel|last3=López-García|first4=Gloria|last4=Cuenca-Bescós|title=Did humans disturb bats? Exploring the hominin-chiropter interactions in the Sierra de Atapuerca sites (early to Middle Pleistocene, Spain)|journal=Quaternary Science Reviews|year= 2019|issn=0277-3791|article-number=106018|volume=226|doi=10.1016/j.quascirev.2019.106018|bibcode=2019QSRv..22606018G }}</ref> The rodent fossils are also well-preserved and show no signs of digestion (not deposited by owl [[pellet (ornithology)|pellets]]), so they probably tunneled in through some small crevice.<ref name=GarciaArsuaga2011/>

The Gran Dolina TD10.1 and Galería GII and GIII sites had: the fallow deer ''[[Dama clactoniana]]'', the [[red deer]], the roe deer ''[[roe deer|Capreolus priscus]]'', the giant deer ''[[Praemegaceros|Praemegaceros solilhacus]]'', the [[narrow-nosed rhinoceros]], the [[wild horse]], the [[European wild ass]], the wood bison ''[[Bison schoetensacki]]'', and the [[Hemitragus bonali|Bonal tahr]]. These herbivores could have been prey items. Like Neanderthals, the Sima de los Huesos hominins may have had a hyper-carnivorous diet comparable to contemporary lions.<ref name=GarciaFeranec2009/><ref name=GarciaArsuaga2011/> Galería seems to have also been a natural trap, and humans were possibly making sporadic, planned trips to the site as a "complementary settlement area" to harvest animals that fell in. TD10.1 was most likely occupied long-term, and the inhabitants seem to have been transporting only the most nutritional parts of a prey item back to the cave.<ref name=MedranoOlle2015/>

The Sima de los Huesos hominins most likely lived during one of the coldest glacial phases of the last million years, which caused an aridification trend in Iberia.<ref name=DemuroArnold2019/> Today, wintertime temperatures of the Sierra de Atapuerca can drop to {{cvt|-10|C}}, and it could have been even colder during glacial periods.<ref name=BartsiokasArsuaga2020/> The mammal assemblage indicates a savannah-like, open woodland environment.<ref name=GarciaFeranec2009/> Both humans and lions seem to have been following the expanding open woodland corridors of Europe. The pollen record also indicates the spread of grass at this time. Aside from grasses, [[pine]] was predominant, followed by [[mesic habitat|mesic]] plants such as [[oak]], [[birch]], and [[beech]].<ref name=GarciaArsuaga2011/> Extensive vertical scratches on the teeth indicate that the Sima de los Huesos hominins were commonly chewing abrasive (dirty) foods, such as unwashed roots and stems. Females tend to have longer scratches in the lower teeth, suggesting their diet may have been different from males.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=Alejandro|last1=Pérez-Pérez|first2=J. M.|last2=Bermúdez De Castro|first3=J.l.|last3=Arsuaga|title=Nonocclusal dental microwear analysis of 300,000-year-old ''Homo heilderbergensis'' Teeth from Sima de los Huesos (Sierra de Atapuerca, Spain)|journal=American Journal of Physical Anthropology|year=1999|issn=1096-8644|pages=433–457|volume=108|issue=4|doi=10.1002/(SICI)1096-8644(199904)108:4<433::AID-AJPA5>3.0.CO;2-5|pmid=10229388 }}</ref>

===Technology===
No [[stone tool]]s were found in the Sima de los Huesos, as it was probably never inhabited. The Galería and Gran Dolina sites, on the other hand, preserve expansive lithic assemblages. Knapping techniques evolved significantly over time, but in general the Galería assemblage fits within the [[Acheulean]] [[industry (archaeology)|industry]], a [[Lower Paleolithic]] technology. TD10.1 could represent the transition to the [[Mousterian]] industry, a [[Middle Paleolithic]] technology associated with Neanderthals.<ref name=MedranoOlle2015>{{cite journal|first1=Paula|last1=García-Medrano|first2=Andreu|last2=Ollé|first3=Marina|last3=Mosquera|first4=Isabel|last4=Cáceres|title=The nature of technological changes: The Middle Pleistocene stone tool assemblages from Galería and Gran Dolina-subunit TD10.1 (Atapuerca, Spain)|journal=Quaternary International|year=2015|issn=1040-6182|pages=95–109|volume=368|series=Groundwater and Cultural Heritage|doi=10.1016/j.quaint.2015.03.006|first5=Eudald|last5=Carbonell|bibcode=2015QuInt.368...92G }}</ref><ref name=OlleMosquera2013/>

[[File:Bifaz de Atapuerca (TG10).jpg|thumb|[[Acheulean]] [[handaxe]] from Trinchera Galería]]
In Galería, there is little [[debitage]] (wastage), suggesting the tools were predominantly made off-site, with only quick, simple [[retouch (lithics)|retouching]] happening onsite. This suggests that the site was used as a temporary base camp. In GIIa (the older part), the tool assemblage is mostly represented by simple [[lithic flake]]s, followed by retouched tools, and unmodified cobble. Retouched tools were usually made using [[chert]] and quartz, and large cutting tools ([[handaxe]]s and [[cleaver (Stone Age tool)|cleavers]]) were predominantly made from [[quartzite]]. Unusually, cobble seems to have been used to shape the larger tools. In GIIb, larger tools (which require more planning) were produced more frequently from pre-prepared flakes instead of cobble, and quartzite is often replaced by [[sandstone]], chert, and limestone.<ref name=OlleMosquera2013/><ref name=MedranoOlle2015/> It is possible GIIb represents an entirely new group from GIIa, with different tool-making traditions.<ref name=MedranoOlle2015/> These trends continue into GIII, but the knappers stop shaping the base of the tool. In GIII, fewer and more efficient strikes were used, cleaving off bigger flakes from a core but making the end product less standardized. The tools are also generally shorter and wider.<ref name=MedranoOlle2015/><ref name=OlleMosquera2013>{{cite journal|first1=Andreu|last1=Ollé|first2=Marina|last2=Mosquera|first3=Xosé Pedro|last3=Rodríguez|first4=Arturo|last4=de Lombera-Hermida|title=The Early and Middle Pleistocene technological record from Sierra de Atapuerca (Burgos, Spain)|journal=Quaternary International|year= 2013|issn=1040-6182|pages=148–155|volume=295|series=East meets West: First settlements and human evolution in Eurasia|doi=10.1016/j.quaint.2011.11.009|first5=María Dolores|last5=García-Antón|first6=Paula|last6=García-Medrano|first7=Luna|last7=Peña|first8=Leticia|last8=Menéndez|first9=Marta|last9=Navazo|first10=Marcos|last10=Terradillos|first11=Amèlia|last11=Bargalló|first12=Belén|last12=Márquez|first13=Robert|last13=Sala|first14=Eudald|last14=Carbonell|bibcode=2013QuInt.295..138O }}</ref>

TD10.1 preserves over 20,000 [[Stone tool|lithics]], one of the archeologically richest sites in the Sierra de Atapuerca. This likely represents long-term occupation sequences, in addition to some short-term ones. Similarly, there is a predominance of flakes and debitage over large cutting tools, as well as a complete [[chaîne opératoire]] (all debitage and products made during the tool-making process are present). TD10.1 is otherwise comparable to GIII. Tools were mainly made of chert but sandstone and quartzite became more popular over time.<ref name=MedranoOlle2015/><ref name=OlleMosquera2013/> Some chert seems to have been collected from a source {{cvt|10|km}} away, an unexpectedly long distance to obtain resources for such an early group of humans. These tools were probably used extensively for butchering, as well as hide- and woodworking activity.<ref name=OlleMosquera2013/> Similarly, dental wearing suggests that every individual was commonly using the mouth as a third hand to bite onto probably animal skin or vegetable fibers with the front teeth, while cutting the material with a tool.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=Marina|last1=Lozano|first2=José M.|last2=Bermúdez de Castro|first3=Eudald|last3=Carbonell|first4=Juan Luis|last4=Arsuaga|title=Non-masticatory uses of anterior teeth of Sima de los Huesos individuals (Sierra de Atapuerca, Spain)|journal=Journal of Human Evolution|year=2008|issn=0047-2484|pages=724–726|volume=55|issue=4|doi=10.1016/j.jhevol.2008.04.007|pmid=18617220 |bibcode=2008JHumE..55..713L |url=https://eprints.ucm.es/id/eprint/12237/1/Lozano_et_al_2008__1_Non_masticatory_uses_of_anterior_teeth_SH_.pdf }}</ref>

Knapping techniques are generally unstandardized, but the gradual shift in raw materials caused the longitudinal method (striking a [[lithic core]] parallel to its long axis, better suited for harder quartzite) to become less common, in favor of the orthogonal method (striking a core perpendicular to its long axis). In Galería, this gradually gets replaced by the centripetal method (striking starts at the edge of the core and works inward) in combination with the longitudinal method. In TD10.1, the centripetal and discoidal methods (associated with the Middle Paleolithic [[Levallois technique]], exercising more control over the final shape) become more popular.<ref name=MedranoOlle2015/><ref name=OlleMosquera2013/>

The Sima de los Huesos hominins were probably not [[control of fire by early humans|using fire]];<ref name=GalanLahuerta2019/> instead physiologically withstanding the cold climate with their large body size, and presumably high activity levels and metabolic heat. High quality evidence of fire usage in Europe appears after an [[interglacial]] during [[Marine Isotope Stage 9]] (roughly 340,000 years ago).<ref>{{cite journal|first1=Katharine|last1=MacDonald|title=The use of fire and human distribution|journal=Temperature|year=2017|issn=2332-8940|pages=157–158|volume=4|issue=2|pmid=28680931|pmc=5489006|doi=10.1080/23328940.2017.1284637}}</ref> A 400,000 year old site in [[Barnham, Suffolk]], has evidence of burned tools and [[iron pyrite]]—a mineral which has, in recent times, been used as a [[fire striker]]. This could suggest that European populations at this time could create fire, but fire creation in non-modern humans is still debated.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=Rob|last1=Davis|first2=Marcus|last2=Hatch|first3=Sally|last3=Hoare|first4=Simon G.|last4=Lewis|title=Earliest evidence of making fire|journal=Nature|year=2025|issn=1476-4687|pages=1–7|doi=10.1038/s41586-025-09855-6|first5=Claire|last5=Lucas|first6=Simon A.|last6=Parfitt|first7=Silvia M.|last7=Bello|first8=Mark|last8=Lewis|first9=Jordan|last9=Mansfield|first10=Jens|last10=Najorka|first11=Simon|last11=O’Connor|first12=Sylvia|last12=Peglar|first13=Andrew|last13=Sorensen|first14=Chris|last14=Stringer|first15=Nick|last15=Ashton}}</ref>

===Burial===
[[File:Hand Axe Sima de los Huesos.jpg|thumb|"Excalibur" was possibly a [[grave goods|grave good]].<ref name=Carbonell2006/>]]
There are many peculiarities in the [[taphonomy]] of the Sima de los Huesos hominins which could suggest that they were intentionally buried by other humans, instead of falling down a natural pitfall as in the case of the many cave bears at the site.<ref name=Carbonell2006/>

About half of the Sima de los Huesos material is represented by adolescents/young adults between 15 and 18 years of age. Infants (below 2 years) are absent, and children below 10 are unusually rare given the high [[infant mortality]] rate of recent hunter-gatherer societies. The few individuals who seem to have surpassed 30 do not seem to have survived into their 40s based on the degree of tooth wearing. The overrepresentation of young adults in their prime (catastrophic mortality [[demographic profile|profile]]) instead of children and elderly (attritional mortality profile) suggests that the accumulation does not represent multiple generations which lived and died in the cave but rather a single high-mortality event. A lack of stone tools also suggests this was not a living space.<ref name=CastroElena1997>{{cite journal|first1=José Maria|last1=Bermúdez de Castro|first2=Marı́a Elena|last2=Nicolás|title=Palaeodemography of the Atapuerca-SH Middle Pleistocene hominid sample|journal=Journal of Human Evolution|year=1997|issn=0047-2484|pages=333–355|volume=33|issue=2|doi=10.1006/jhev.1997.0110|pmid=9300346 |bibcode=1997JHumE..33..333B }}</ref><ref name=TorresLozano2004>{{cite journal|first1=María|last1=Martinón-Torres|first2=Marina|last2=Lozano|first3=Susana|last3=Sarmiento|first4=Ana|last4=Muela|title=Paleodemography of the Atapuerca: Sima De Los Huesos Hominin Sample: A Revision and New Approaches to the Paleodemography of the European Middle Pleistocene Population|journal=Journal of Anthropological Research|year= 2004|issn=0091-7710|pages=5–26|volume=60|issue=1|doi=10.1086/jar.60.1.3631006}}</ref><ref name=CastroMartinez2020/> Because the entire skeleton (including fragile pieces) is extremely well represented by numerous different individuals all found in the same narrow layer of sediment, the bodies were most likely deposited in the Sima de los Huesos completely intact at around the same time. They also by-and-large lack carnivore damage.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/235642421|first1=Juan Luis|last1=Arsuaga|first2=José Miguel|last2=Carretero|first3=Ana|last3=Gracia|first4=Ignacio|last4=Martínez|year=1990|title=Taphonomical analysis of the human sample from the Sima de los Huesos Middle Pleistocene site (Atapuerca/Ibeas, Spain)|journal=Human Evolution|volume=5|issue=6|pages=505–513}}</ref><ref name=SalaMartinez2024>{{cite journal|first1=Nohemi|last1=Sala|first2=Ignacio|last2=Martínez|first3=Carlos|last3=Lorenzo|first4=Rebeca|last4=García|title=Taphonomic skeletal disturbances in the Sima de los Huesos postcranial remains|journal=The Anatomical Record|year=2024 |issn=1932-8494|pages=2447–2448|volume=307|issue=7|doi=10.1002/ar.25197|first5=José Miguel|last5=Carretero|first6=Laura|last6=Rodríguez|first7=Asier|last7=Gómez-Olivencia|first8=Arantza|last8=Aranburu|first9=Nuria|last9=García|first10=Rolf|last10=Quam|first11=Ana|last11=Gracia|first12=Mª Cruz|last12=Ortega|first13=Juan Luis|last13=Arsuaga|pmid=36877151 }}</ref><ref name=Carbonell2006/><ref name=CastroMartinez2020/> Because Cranium 17 presents two identical fatal injuries (therefore presumably caused by the same hard object), this individual was likely already killed — maybe by another human — before being deposited in the Sima de los Huesos.<ref name=ArsuagaMartinez2024/> 

Additionally, a single Acheulean handaxe (nicknamed "Excalibur") was deposited with the bodies, the only lithic artifact found at the site. It is made of high-quality [[vein (geology)|veined]] quartzite, which was rarely used in the region, and was quite large at {{cvt|155 × 97 × 58|mm}} and  {{cvt|685|g|lb|1}}. It lacks any indication of wearing or usage, unless it was scrubbed away by sand over time. In the context of intentional burial, Carbonell and colleagues suggested it was left as a [[grave goods|grave good]] — an early example of complex symbolic thinking.<ref name=Carbonell2006/>

===Language===
It is possible that the Sima de los Huesos hominins were speaking with some [[origin of language|early form of language]], especially considering the evidence of intentional burial and symbolic thinking.<ref name=Carbonell2006>{{cite journal|first1=E. |last1=Carbonell |first2=M. |last2=Mosquera |year=2006 |title=The emergence of a symbolic behaviour: the sepulchral pit of Sima de los Huesos, Sierra de Atapuerca, Burgos, Spain |journal=Comptes Rendus Palevol |volume=5 |issue=1–2 |pages=155–160 |doi=10.1016/j.crpv.2005.11.010|bibcode=2006CRPal...5..155C }}</ref> The Sima de los Huesos hominins had a modern humanlike [[hyoid bone]] (which supports the tongue), but this trait can exist without language and humanlike speech capacity.<ref name=MartinezArsuaga2008>{{cite journal|first1=I. |last1=Martínez |first2=J. L. |last2=Arsuaga |author-link2=Juan Luis Arsuaga |first3=R. |last3=Quam |display-authors=et al. |year=2008 |title=Human hyoid bones from the middle Pleistocene site of the Sima de los Huesos (Sierra de Atapuerca, Spain) |journal=[[Journal of Human Evolution]] |volume=54 |issue=1 |pages=118–124 |doi=10.1016/j.jhevol.2007.07.006 |pmid=17804038 |bibcode=2008JHumE..54..118M |url=https://eprints.ucm.es/id/eprint/26853/1/1-s2.0-S0047_1.pdf }}</ref> Judging by dental striations, they seem to have been predominantly right-handed, and handedness is related to the [[lateralisation of brain function]], typically associated with language processing in modern humans.<ref name=LozanoMosquera2009>{{cite journal |last1=Lozano |first1=Marina |last2=Mosquera |first2=Marina |last3=De Castro |first3=José María Bermúdez |last4=Arsuaga |first4=Juan Luis |last5=Carbonell |first5=Eudald |year=2009 |title=Right handedness of ''Homo heidelbergensis'' from Sima de los Huesos (Atapuerca, Spain) 500,000 years ago |journal=[[Evolution and Human Behavior]] |volume=30 |issue=5 |pages=369–376 |doi=10.1016/j.evolhumbehav.2009.03.001|bibcode=2009EHumB..30..369L }}</ref>

The [[ossicles|middle ear bones]] are comparable to Neanderthals and modern humans, maybe suggesting they could distinguish the higher frequencies necessary to discern speech (2–4 [[hertz|kHz]]).<ref>{{cite journal|first1=I.|last1=Martínez|first2=M.|last2=Rosa|first3=R.|last3=Quam|first4=P.|last4=Jarabo|title=Communicative capacities in Middle Pleistocene humans from the Sierra de Atapuerca in Spain|journal=Quaternary International|year=2013|issn=1040-6182|pages=94–101|volume=295|series=East meets West: First settlements and human evolution in Eurasia|doi=10.1016/j.quaint.2012.07.001|first5=C.|last5=Lorenzo|first6=A.|last6=Bonmatí|first7=A.|last7=Gómez-Olivencia|first8=A.|last8=Gracia|first9=J. L.|last9=Arsuaga|bibcode=2013QuInt.295...94M }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|first1=I.|last1=Martínez|first2=M.|last2=Rosa|first3=J.-L.|last3=Arsuaga|first4=P.|last4=Jarabo|title=Auditory capacities in Middle Pleistocene humans from the Sierra de Atapuerca in Spain|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|year=2004|pages=9976–9981|volume=101|issue=27|pmid=15213327|pmc=454200|doi=10.1073/pnas.0403595101|first5=R.|last5=Quam|first6=C.|last6=Lorenzo|first7=A.|last7=Gracia|first8=J.-M.|last8=Carretero|first9=J.-M. Bermúdez|last9=de Castro|first10=E.|last10=Carbonell|doi-access=free |bibcode=2004PNAS..101.9976M }}</ref> Still, the functional anatomy of the ear suggests that the Sima de los Huesos hominins had different hearing capacities than Neanderthals and modern humans. Like [[chimpanzee]]s, the [[ear canal]] is long, and the [[eardrum]] and [[oval window]] are small and at a low angle. Uniquely, the [[tympanic cavity]] (which contains the middle ear bones) and [[aditus to mastoid antrum|aditus]] are large. The [[cochlea]] (which affects hearing) is more constricted than in Neanderthals in the first turn (of about three turns), reminiscent of chimpanzees. Like in Neanderthals and modern humans, the third turn is short but is more strongly curved.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=Mercedes|last1=Conde-Valverde|first2=Ignacio|last2=Martínez|first3=Rolf|last3=Quam|first4=Juan Luis|last4=Arsuaga|title=The ear of the Sima de los Huesos hominins (Atapuerca, Spain)|journal=The Anatomical Record|year=2022|issn=1932-8494|pages=2410–2424|volume=307|issue=7|doi=10.1002/ar.25181|pmid=36825485 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name=VelezQuam2023>{{cite journal|first1=Alex D.|last1=Velez|first2=Rolf|last2=Quam|first3=Mercedes|last3=Conde-Valverde|first4=Ignacio|last4=Martínez|title=Geometric morphometric analysis of the bony labyrinth of the Sima de los Huesos hominins|journal=Journal of Human Evolution|year= 2023|issn=0047-2484|pages=2418–2422|volume=174|doi=10.1016/j.jhevol.2022.103280|first5=Carlos|last5=Lorenzo|first6=Juan Luis|last6=Arsuaga|article-number=103280 |pmid=36455404 |bibcode=2023JHumE.17403280V }}</ref>
